content.text: The text reviews cholera infantum, pseudo-membranous enteritis, dysentery, typhlitis, intestinal ulcers, hemorrhage, and obstruction. Cholera infantum causes profuse watery diarrhea, vomiting, thirst, rapid dehydration, emaciation, collapse, and sometimes death; prevention and treatment emphasize breast milk, safe feeding, clean air, hydration, and careful medicines. Pseudo-membranous enteritis is a chronic, chiefly female disorder involving recurrent mucous casts. Dysentery causes colonic inflammation, tenesmus, pain, mucus, blood, and possible hepatic or systemic complications; sanitation, rest, diet, irrigation, and ipecacuanha are discussed. Typhlitis centers on the cecum or appendix and may lead to abscess or perforation. Ulcers, intestinal bleeding, and obstruction may arise from infection, trauma, tumors, concretions, torsion, or intussusception. An infant hospital ship carried sick children down the bay to fresh ocean air; patients were also advised to move to rural or coastal areas.
